summary: This experimental memo describes Sender-Initiated File Transfer, also called Unsolicited File Transfer, a protocol where the sender pushes a file to a recipient without being asked.

eli5.summary: Most file sharing is you asking for a file. Here the sender pushes it to you, like dropping a package on your doorstep.

subtitle: A protocol for the sender to push a file to a recipient over TCP

tldr.problem: In early file transfer systems, the recipient must request a file. This model does not suit all use cases, particularly for non-correspondence file transfer where the sender wants to push data to a recipient without prior negotiation.
tldr.mechanism: SIFT/UFT (Sender-Initiated/Unsolicited File Transfer) operates on TCP port 608. The client connects and sends a control file (plain text commands) followed by a data file (binary). The server responds to each command with an ACK or NAK.
tldr.outcome: This enables push-based file transfer without sender authentication or accounts on the target system. Files wait in a staging area for the recipient to accept or reject them.

today: RFC 1440 remains Experimental and was never widely deployed. Modern file transfer relies on HTTP/HTTPS, cloud storage, FTP/SFTP, and email with large attachment support. The concept of sender-initiated push transfer has re-emerged in modern protocols and APIs, but UFT itself is obsolete.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
RFC 1440 describes the Sender-Initiated File Transfer (SIFT) protocol, also called Unsolicited File Transfer (UFT). Unlike traditional file transfer, SIFT does not require the sender to have an account or credentials on the receiving system. The sender connects and pushes file(s) to the recipient, who retrieves them when ready from a staging area.

The protocol suits background or deferred operation. This capability came from non-IP networks like BITNET, which supported sending files as parcels rather than mail. The RFC author argues that electronic mail is poorly suited for non-correspondence file transfer, and that a dedicated protocol would fill a gap in the TCP/IP suite.
sections.eli5: SIFT lets the sender push a file to a receiver without the receiver asking for it, and without needing an account on the system. It is like a package delivery service built into the network.

sections.title: Connection and Protocol Flow
sections.content:
A server listens on TCP port 608 for inbound connections. When a client connects, the server immediately sends a herald message indicating the hostname, protocol version, and server version. For example: 100 ricevm1.rice.edu UFT 1.0 VM/CMS-0.9.2 ready.

One TCP connection carries both commands and data. The client sends commands as ASCII text lines terminated by CR/LF. After each command, the server responds with either an ACK (a single NULL byte) or a NAK (any other byte or silence). When the client issues a DATA command, the server switches to binary data mode and reads the specified number of octets, then returns to command mode.
sections.eli5: The client dials the server on port 608. The server says hello and what version it is. Then the client sends commands one by one, and the server says yes or no to each.

sections.title: Commands and File Parameters
sections.content:
A SIFT transaction requires several commands. The FILE command specifies the size of the data (in bytes, with optional M, K, or G multiplier) and the sender's login name. The USER command names the local recipient or service. The TYPE command specifies the data representation: ASCII (A), binary (B), fixed-length records (F), variable-length records with 16-bit lengths (V), and many others borrowed from BITNET and IBM mainframe conventions.

Optional commands include NAME (the filename at the destination), DATE (timestamp in mm/dd/yy hh:mm:ss format), and print-related commands like CLASS, FORM, and CHARSET for print jobs. The DATA command signals the start of the file contents. The EOF command closes the file and returns to command mode. The ABORT command discards the file. The QUIT command ends the session.
sections.eli5: The client tells the server: how much data (FILE), who gets it (USER), what format (TYPE), and any other details. Then DATA starts the actual file bytes.

sections.title: File Staging and Delivery
sections.content:
When files arrive at the destination, they are held in a public staging area (such as /usr/spool/uft) until the recipient accepts or rejects them, or the system discards them for age. This staging area is shared space, managed by the system. How long files remain unprocessed and how large they may grow are local administrative decisions.

The server treats incoming data with minimal processing until the recipient acts. Multiple files can be sent in one session using multiple DATA commands separated by EOF or ABORT commands. The fast mode allows the client to omit the burst-size parameter from DATA, in which case the connection remains open until the client closes it, sending all remaining data as one file.
sections.eli5: Files arrive in a staging area like a mailbox. The recipient picks them up when they want to. The server does not process them until the recipient accepts them.

sections.title: TCP and Mail Encapsulation
sections.content:
SIFT natively operates over TCP. However, not all hosts have IP connectivity, and some are behind firewalls that pass only mail. For such hosts, UFT can be carried as MIME Content-Type: application/octet-stream within email. In this case, UFT commands become parameters in the Content-Type header, and the data file is BASE64-encoded in the mail body.

When transported via mail, the data file must be encoded since mail is text-based, but the commands remain human-readable in the header. This dual-transport design lets UFT reach hosts isolated from the network while still supporting direct TCP operation where available.
sections.eli5: SIFT uses TCP when it can. If a computer is behind a mail firewall, SIFT can hide inside an email message instead.

sections.title: Authentication and Implementation Notes
sections.content:
The AUTH token in the FILE command is unimplemented in the RFC. Authentication is not ensured by the protocol as described. The author notes that several approaches could add authentication, but defers implementation to future developments. When UFT is piggybacked on mail, authentication is left to the mail transfer system's mechanisms.

Job Entry capability allows the target user to be a service or queue rather than a human user, enabling batch processing and job submission workflows. The RFC explicitly states that security issues are not discussed; implementations must add protection such as access controls, file validation, and limits on resource use in the staging area.
sections.eli5: The protocol does not include strong authentication. Senders identify themselves with a login name, but nothing verifies they are who they claim. Implementations must add their own security.
